name: Right Model, Right Task: Capability-Constrained Carbon Labeling to Decarbonize Generative AI
headline: Right Model, Right Task: Capability-Constrained Carbon Labeling to Decarbonize Generative AI
abstract: The carbon footprint of generative-AI inference depends not only on hardware efficiency and electricity supply, but also on whether the selected model is appropriate for the task. A frontier model may expend unnecessary computation on a routine request, whereas an under-capable model may increase energy use through failure, retries, extended reasoning and escalation. However, a standardized evaluation framework that accounts for task-specific capability requirements and the carbon emissions associated with successful task remains lacking. In this Perspective, we argue for a capability-constrained carbon labeling framework that shifts environmental assessment from carbon intensity per inference towards the expected carbon emissions per successfully completed task at the required capability level. Under this framework, models would first be assessed against task-specific capability requirements, and only models capable of meeting those requirements would be compared on their expected energy use and operational carbon emissions. By linking service quality to carbon cost, this approach could enable more informed matching of the right model to the right task, offering a demand-side pathway to reducing emissions associated with generative-AI token use. Realizing this vision will require standardized capability-based service assessments, comprehensive energy accounting and transparent carbon disclosures.

description: Qu et al. (2026), arXiv:2610.35189, propose capability-constrained carbon labeling for generative AI and large language model (LLM) selection under task quality constraints. Models first need to meet the task's required capability; eligible configurations are then compared by expected operational carbon emissions per successfully completed task. The accounting includes failures, retries and escalation to a more capable model, together with deployment-specific electricity carbon intensity. This Perspective connects model–task matching, carbon-aware LLM routing and task-success-based inference evaluation. Its illustrative 2025 comparison estimates 16.9 Mt CO₂ for task-matched selection versus 47.0 Mt CO₂ for reconstructed current use, a reported 64.0% reduction under the assumed conditions. The work proposes an evaluation framework and scenarios; it does not release a benchmark dataset, validate a universal model ranking or demonstrate a production router.

about.name: Model–task matching; task-appropriate model selection
about.description: Selecting models that meet explicit task-specific capability or quality requirements before comparing carbon cost.

about.name: Carbon-aware LLM routing; model escalation
about.description: Routing is a potential use of the proposed labels. Accounting includes failed attempts, retries and escalation; this Perspective does not implement a production router.

about.name: Task success rate; emissions per successful task
about.description: Task performance defines eligibility, and successful completion is the service unit for carbon comparison. Per-token or per-call energy alone does not establish equivalent service quality.

about.name: Inference energy benchmark methodology; quality constraints
about.description: The paper identifies evaluation and reporting requirements for capability, energy and deployment-specific carbon accounting. It proposes a framework rather than a released benchmark suite.
